newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Deflation in Brazil? Yes, but not for long.
newsitem.headline: Deflation in Brazil? Yes, but not for long.

text.p: Brazil, once ravaged by high inflation, has posted its first decline in consumer prices in years, but economists warn it is not a sign of things to come.

Consumer prices measured by the Getulio Vargas Foundation's IGP-M index fell 0.40 percent between August 21-31, the first time the index posted a decline in consumer prices since its creation in 1989.
"This number was really surprising, but the index is very volatile. It does not mean we will be in a period of deflation," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist at J.P. Morgan in Brazil.
The IGP-M index, which also includes separate indices for wholesale and construction prices, measures one 10-day period against the previous and serves as a preview for monthly inflation.

Although most economists were reluctant to predict further consumer price declines, some participants in a recent Reuter survey said the IGP-M index as a whole could fall slightly in September. The average forecast is for a 0.19 percent rise.
Even if the price index rises slightly, Brazil's inflation outlook is promising, economists said.

"We might not get deflation for the month, but the recent numbers are a good sign because they show that the economic recovery is not fueling price hikes," said Mauro Schneider, chief economist at ING Bank in Brazil.
"This means Brazil can have economic growth with low inflation, which Argentina has not been able to manage," Schneider said.

The IGP-M index measures inflation throughout Brazil, unlike the closely watched Fipe index which only measures the variation of consumer prices in the city of Sao Paulo. The Fipe index has not registered a single case of monthly deflation since the 1950s.

Brazil's two-year-old anti-inflation drive, known as the Real Plan, has wrestled price increases down to their lowest levels in decades from 50 percent monthly price jumps. The benchmark Fipe index rose just 23 percent in 1995, the lowest rate in more than two decades.
Economists say the Fipe index will rise by between 11 and 13 percent in 1996.
